# Global Supply Chain Resilience & Responsible Sourcing Programme
## Recommendation for the Steering Group

**Version 2.0 — complete. No section is deferred; where a number cannot honestly be fixed before the diagnostic reports, it is shown as a gate parameter with the date and the person who will set it (§12.6, §16).**

**Circulation:** steering group, for decision. Prior circulation to the seven category leads, the four plant directors, Group Legal, Group Trade Compliance, Group Reporting and the Chief Financial Officer's office. **Not yet for supplier communication. Expressly not yet for any external, customer-facing or investor-facing statement** (§10.1).

---

### How we would ask you to use this

Three notes, then the substance.

**First, what changed from v1.0 and why.** The reviewers were right on three points that went to the design rather than to the drafting, and we would rather record that plainly than absorb it quietly.

1. v1.0 offered a single waiver route across all five floors. That was wrong. A standard concerning forced labour cannot carry a waiver, and an internal register recording that an officer of this company approved a twelve-month departure from one would be a document read back to us in a customs proceeding or an NGO report. The floors are now split into **two classes** — non-derogable and progressive — and only the progressive class has a flexibility route, which is now a dated closure plan rather than a waiver (§3, §3.8).
2. The disclosure amnesty in v1.0 promised more than we are lawfully able to promise. It now covers **commercial consequence only**, with scheduled legal exclusions, material substitution removed to its own route, a concealment carve-out, and a records architecture to be agreed with Legal and the external auditor before a single supplier hears the word (§3.7).
3. The failure test was built on AND-logic and could almost never have fired. It is now OR-logic on the substantive proxies, with coverage-based rather than absolute-dollar metrics, and with thresholds set after the diagnostic produces a baseline rather than invented before it (§8.6).

**Second, the cards.** The cluster cards in §6 are **working hypotheses about supply structures and site conditions, offered so that they can be corrected**. They describe patterns we have observed in supply flows, not countries and not the people who live in them. Where a category lead or plant holds real diagnostic data — an unannounced assessment, a worker-voice sample, a qualification study — that data supersedes the card and the card is retired for that flow (§5.4). A card returned unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet taken place, and we would come back for it.

**Third, two courtesies we would ask the steering group to extend before this travels further.**

- That the seven category leads, the four plant directors and the two engineering chiefs see §§3, 4, 9 and 13 and have time to respond in their own way, through their own line, before the board pack is assembled. A programme that devolves sourcing judgement and then arrives in a category fully formed has already contradicted itself, and colleagues will notice that before they notice anything else.
- That §10 be walked through with Group Legal, Trade Compliance, Group Reporting and the external auditor **before any part of this is described to a supplier**, and that no wording from this paper migrate into a sustainability statement, customer questionnaire response or investor deck without the sign-off route in §10.1. The single likeliest cause of avoidable damage here is not a supply failure. It is a well-meant public commitment that becomes a disclosure liability, or a supplier questionnaire that creates a written record we cannot later stand behind.

*A note on suppliers themselves: v1.0 designed a supplier-facing architecture without consulting a supplier, while arguing that programmes arriving fully formed contradict themselves. That inconsistency is corrected in §11.5 — a supplier advisory panel of nine, convened before Gate 2, with two seats reserved for Tier-2 firms.*

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a thin global core and a wide local expression: five sourcing floors, split into non-derogable and progressive classes; supplier selection, remediation sequencing, buffer design and local partnership devolved to categories and plants beneath a mandatory-uniform contract layer and single-point supplier ownership; a bounded disclosure amnesty that treats supplier-found problems as intelligence; an engineering design-for-resilience workstream, because single-sourcing is created at specification and not in procurement; four instrumented pilots; and a published protocol binding our own buying conduct to the same discipline we ask of suppliers. Approve the diagnostic and mobilisation now; approve the full envelope at a named gate when the baseline exists.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Scale anchor** (absent from v1.0) | Revenue $4.1B; COGS $2.94B; direct materials and components spend **$1.42B**; 1,834 Tier-1 suppliers across 38 countries; 4 plants; 7 categories. Indicative full-programme spend of $17.6M Y1 is **1.24% of direct spend** and **0.43% of revenue** **[O]** |
| Global mandate — **Class A, non-derogable** | Freely-given labour and worker-pays-nothing (Floor II core indicators); prohibition of retaliation against a worker who raises a concern (Floor III core). **No waiver, no register entry, no alternative form.** Escalation and remediation only (§3.3, §3.4) |
| Global mandate — **Class B, progressive** | Traceability depth of critical flows; grievance-channel maturity; qualified-alternative capability; responsible-exit sequencing. Each has a **dated closure plan** route, approved and reviewed, never an open-ended waiver (§3.8) |
| Devolved to categories & plants | Supplier choice within the approved-vendor frame, remediation sequencing, buffer sizing, local partners, capability-building design, and the language in which any of it is described to suppliers — beneath a **mandatory-uniform contract layer** and **single-point supplier ownership** (§4.5) |
| The engineering half | **Design-for-resilience workstream** co-owned by Engineering: second-source-ready specification standard, part standardisation, qualification-cycle compression, dual-tooling policy at part-approval gate (§7.5). This was the largest omission in v1.0 |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots** — one deep-tier opaque flow; one single-source long-qualification part; one high-agency-labour site cluster; one recently-acquired plant's inherited supply base — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§7) |
| Principal risk | **Our own procurement and forecasting incentives**, not supplier resistance (§8.1). Cost-down targets, forecast bias and change-order volatility will defeat this faster than any supplier will **[J]** |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published buyer-conduct protocol**, quarterly: our forecast bias by category, payment-term behaviour, audit visits imposed per supplier, change-order frequency, and every reversal of a devolved sourcing decision with written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision (§9) |
| Element we would defend | **12-month bounded disclosure amnesty** (§3.7): commercial consequence waived for self-disclosed Tier-2s, recruitment-fee findings and labour findings; legal consequence never waived; scheduled exclusions; substitution excluded and routed to Quality (§3.7.3) **[J]** |
| Measurement | 70% operational and worker-verified proxies, 30% declared and audit scores **[J]**; audit-score inflation correction with a **stated method** — unannounced-audit delta, worker-voice divergence coefficient, auditor-firm fixed effects, shrinkage on small n (§8.4) |
| Numeric failure test | **OR-logic**, five substantive conditions; a rising audited-compliance index is an **aggravating** condition, not a gate. Thresholds set at Gate 2 from the diagnostic baseline. Firing the test pauses the programme and stops further capital (§8.6) |
| Money — one view, not two | **Total cost of ownership, Years 1–3: $58.7M**, comprising programme opex $29.7M; buffer and qualification-inventory carrying and obsolescence cost $9.4M; one-off working-capital build $46M (balance sheet, ~$19.6M residual after Y3 unwind). Funding routes and governance differ and are shown separately **on the same page** (§12.2) |
| Of which supplier capability funding **we** pay | **$5.8M** across two years — the line most often cut first, and the one whose absence has ended comparable programmes elsewhere **[J]** |
| Funding split | Central funds diagnostic, traceability platform, upstream mapping, worker-voice channels, remedy fund, pilot facilitation. Plants and categories fund qualification and dual-tooling with a **65% central offset in Y1, 35% in Y2, nil thereafter** **[J]** (§12.4) |
| Decision architecture | **Two gates, not one.** Gate 1 on **22 April**: approve $2.41M for diagnostic, mobilisation, engineering scoping, worker-voice pilot and legal records architecture. Gate 2 on **15 July**: full envelope, pilot scope, critical-input list, failure thresholds (§12.6) |
| Decisions requested now | **Three** — §12.7 |
| Governance | CPO sponsor; COO co-accountable; **CFO joins the steering group** (working capital); **Chief Sustainability & Reporting Officer joins** (CSRD/disclosure); named tiebreak to the CEO on the two decisions we expect to stall (§10.7, §12.8). Programme director reports to the CPO with a dotted line to the COO, sits in Group Strategy, holds delegated authority to $500K (§12.8) |
| Immediate actions requiring no approval | Four, owners named, all closed within 30 days (§1.3) — including the **54 Tier-1 suppliers who never signed the code and continued to supply** |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Resilience is a purchased option rather than an attitude; and responsible sourcing is an information problem before it is a compliance problem. **[J]** — considered practitioner assertion, not a finding. The steering group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement; the key is at §14 and is now applied throughout rather than decoratively.

The failure we are trying to avoid is documented in our own last three years: a supplier code signed by 1,780 of 1,834 Tier-1 suppliers **[O]**; an audit pass rate above 90% **[O]**; and two disruptions in eighteen months that neither the code nor the audits anticipated, both originating below Tier 1 **[O]**, with combined recovery cost of $23.6M and 41 days of line stoppage across two plants **[O]**. That combination is not a coverage gap. It is evidence that we have measured the wrong things accurately.

### 1.2 What we are not claiming

We are not claiming that this programme prevents disruption. It shortens recovery and reduces the number of surprises **[J]**. We are not claiming it makes the supply base ethical; it makes conditions in it visible and gives us a route to act, which is a smaller and more honest claim **[J]**. And we are not claiming the floors are enforceable at every tier — §4.2 sets out, tier by tier, where we hold leverage and where a floor is honestly **observational** rather than enforceable. v1.0 blurred that line, and blurring it would have embarrassed us in front of the very colleagues we need.

### 1.3 Four things we would close before the steering group next meets

These need no funding and no decision. We list them because the steering group would reasonably ask why they were not already done, and because it would be poor form to hold them inside an eight-figure proposal.

| # | Action | Owner | By |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **The 54 unsigned Tier-1 suppliers.** Establish, supplier by supplier, whether each still supplies, what it supplies, whether any sit on the critical list, why signature was never obtained, and whether a purchase order was placed without terms. Report by name to the steering group | Head of Supplier Governance | 21 days |
| 2 | Confirm which of our own customer contracts contain flow-down clauses that would be breached, or notification obligations triggered, by anything in §3.7 (amnesty) before any supplier hears of it | Group Legal | 30 days |
| 3 | Baseline our own payment-term behaviour against contracted terms by category, and our forecast bias over eight quarters. This is the raw material for §9 and we should know it before we ask anyone else anything | Group Treasury with Category Planning | 30 days |
| 4 | Confirm whether any part on the current critical list is sourced from a site subject to UFLPA entity-list exposure or an equivalent designation | Trade Compliance | 14 days |

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would ask the steering group to test

The initiative is described as *supply chain resilience and ethics*. The evidence available to us may instead describe a **visibility and decision-latency** problem in a resilience costume, compounded by an incentive problem of our own making. Only some of the candidate drivers below respond to supplier requirements, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver | What a code, audit programme and clause cascade do to it | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| We do not know who is in Tier 2–4 for critical flows | Nothing — requires paid mapping and a reason to disclose (§3.7) | **[O]** both 2023–24 disruptions |
| We know, but the information does not reach the person who could act | **Amplifies harm** — confident sourcing decisions on stale data | **[A]** to be tested |
| Single-source parts with multi-year qualification cycles | Nothing — needs capital, tooling and engineering time, not policy | **[O]** 61 parts, mean qualification 9.4 months |
| Single-sourcing designed in at specification stage | Nothing — belongs to Engineering, not Procurement (§7.5) | **[J]** |
| Suppliers have capability gaps rather than intent gaps | Improves *only if* paired with funded capability support (§8.5) | **[A]** |
| Our cost-down targets pay suppliers to conceal problems | Noth

# Global Employee Empowerment & Adaptive Culture Initiative
## Guidance on Regional Leadership Adaptation — Recommendation for Sponsor Group

**Version 2.0 — complete. Prepared for sponsor group decision, and for prior circulation to the fourteen regional people leads. Not yet for employee communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note only, and then the substance.

This version differs from v1.0 in three ways that the reviewers were right to insist on. It now asks for specific decisions, with money and a date attached (§12). It answers the questions the first draft deferred — most importantly what the centre itself is bound by (§9). And the regional material has been re-cut so that no colleague opens it and finds their country described inside someone else's card.

The regional cards in §6 remain what they were: **working hypotheses, offered so that they can be corrected**. Where a region has its own diagnostic data, that data replaces the card and the card is retired for that unit (§5.4). A card returned to us unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet taken place, and we would come back for it.

Two courtesies we would ask the sponsor group to extend before this travels further. First, that the fourteen regional people leads and the four regional MDs see §§3, 4 and 9 and have time to respond in their own way before the board pack is assembled — a programme about devolved authority that arrives in a region fully formed has already contradicted itself, and colleagues will notice that before they notice anything else. Second, that §10 (consultation and legal gates) be walked through with Group Legal, the European Works Council secretariat and Group Reward before any part of this is described to employees anywhere. The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a well-intentioned announcement that reaches a works council after it reaches a newspaper, or reaches an employee before it reaches their own supervisor.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a thin global core and a wide local expression: four employee entitlements defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form process where a floor cannot lawfully or structurally be met; delivery method, language, sequencing and naming devolved entirely to regions; four instrumented pilots in Year 1 with a common measurement spine but deliberately different local design; and a published protocol binding the centre to the same discipline it asks of others.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Global mandate | **Four entitlements only** (§3) — decision rights at the lowest competent level; an answered route for dissent; tolerance of good-faith error; employee-initiated internal movement. Each stated as a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to regions | Language, ritual, sequencing, symbolism, manager incentives, pace, communication channels, and the programme's name. We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the name |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one high-authority-distance, one low, one deskless-majority, one recently-acquired entity** — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§7) |
| Principal risk | Middle-manager status and grade loss, not employee resistance (§8) |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published reversal protocol**: the centre may reverse a devolved decision, but must give written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, and reversal counts are reported quarterly beside regional metrics (§9) |
| Measurement | Within-region trend on four behavioural proxies weighted 70%, survey items 30%; acquiescence correction applied before any cross-region view is shown (§8.3) |
| Numeric failure test | Empowerment survey index +5 points or more while decision latency on the instrumented decision class improves <10% and internal-move rate is flat = declared failure, programme paused, no further capital (§8.5) |
| Investment sought | **$14.2M Year 1, $10.6M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions in §12.1), of which $6.9M is manager time relief — the line most often omitted and most often fatal |
| Funding split | Central P&L funds diagnostic, instrumentation, platform, central team and pilot facilitation; regions fund manager time with a **60% central offset in Y1, 30% in Y2, nil thereafter** (§12.3) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §12.5, sought at the sponsor group meeting on **18 March** |
| Programme owner | Group Chief People Officer, sponsor; named programme director recruited internally within 30 days of approval |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Empowerment mechanisms do not transfer between contexts; the conditions that make them work can be built in each. *(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience, not a finding — see the evidence key at §14. We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented in our own past programmes: exported behavioural vocabulary — "speak up", "own it", "disagree and commit" — produces regions that become fluent at the annual survey and unchanged on Tuesday morning. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would require.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The initiative is currently described as culture change. The evidence available to us may instead describe a **decision-rights and information-flow** problem wearing culture-change clothing. Only one of those two responds to leadership behaviour work, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver | What leadership/empowerment training does to it |
|---|---|
| Decision rights formally held too high | Nothing — requires delegation-of-authority redesign |
| Rights delegated on paper, retracted in practice | Nothing until retraction is made visible and costly (§9) |
| Information does not reach the level holding authority | **Amplifies harm** — confident decisions on poor data |
| Managers lack coaching capability | Improves, *if* paired with funded time relief (§8.4) |
| Reward and grading pay for control, not for developing others | Nothing — the incentive wins every time (§8.2) |
| Employees have voice but no evidence it is ever acted on | Worsens — a further unanswered invitation deepens cynicism |
| Working-language barrier suppresses contribution | Nothing — needs channel design, not confidence-building (§11.1) |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Five weeks, no design freeze until it reports: 60 structured conversations across four organisational levels in eight countries (including two deskless-majority sites); an audit of the documented delegation-of-authority matrix against actual practice in twelve units; and a language-barrier check in the four sites where the working language is not the local one. Cost **$310K**.

If it finds that decision rights are formally too high, the largest part of the Year 2 training envelope should be redirected to delegation architecture and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, now answered rather than deferred

Will headquarters be bound by the same four entitlements? If regional colleagues discover that the centre reserves the right to overturn devolved decisions without giving reasons, the initiative becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. v1.0 left this open. **§9 now answers it with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism**, and we would ask the sponsor group to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what an employee is entitled to, not as how a manager must behave, so that very different conduct can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — decision rights sit at the lowest competent level
**Floor:** every employee can name the classes of decision they own and point to a recent instance of exercising one without seeking permission. *Competent* is doing real work in that sentence; this is not an argument for uniform flat structures.

### 3.2 Entitlement II — there is a route for dissent, and it is answered
**Floor:** every employee has at least one available channel through which they can contradict a superior's view **and receive a response**. The channel may be a written pre-read, a skip-level, a facilitated small group, a mentor, a shift huddle, or an anonymous board. It need never be a raised hand in a large meeting. The answered part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a statutory reporting channel. Disagreement about a business decision is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§10.3).

### 3.3 Entitlement III — good-faith error is absorbed, not attributed
**Floor:** within each unit, at least one specific, visible instance per quarter in which a good-faith mistake was absorbed rather than attributed, and the team can name it. Demonstrated, never announced. In several regions this must be framed collectively rather than individually to be usable at all (§6).

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — employees can initiate their own movement
**Floor (revised from v1.0):** an employee may apply for an internal role, project or rotation **without the incumbent manager holding a veto and without the manager being informed in advance of the application**.

v1.0 stated this as an absolute and was wrong to. In parts of the Gulf, mobility between entities is constrained by employer-tied work permits and is a legal matter, not a cultural one. In Japan, Korea and Taiwan, seniority-anchored career and reward structures make unrestricted lateral self-nomination structurally disruptive in ways that a global mandate cannot responsibly overrule from a distance. The floor above is the most we can hold everywhere; where even that cannot be met, §3.6 applies.

### 3.5 Everything else is regional property
Language, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, incentives, cadence, and the programme's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any region to refuse. A region that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to say what it would take to close the remainder.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not discomfort) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | **Group Chief People Officer**, countersigned by the Regional MD and by Group Legal |
| Duration | **12 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in an internally published register, reviewed quarterly by the sponsor group |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless it is materially weaker than the floor. We expect four to eight across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general culture model

We would ask each region to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given mechanism functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Authority basis** | Does a manager's authority derive from role or from demonstrated expertise? | Whether devolution reads as trust or as abandonment |
| **Directness of disagreement** | Can dissent be public without cost to either party? | The design of the dissent channel (Entitlement II) |
| **Attribution of error** | Does a mistake attach to a person, a team, or a system? | Whether error tolerance can be individual or must be collective (III) |
| **Ambiguity tolerance** | Is an open brief experienced as freedom, or as information withheld? | How much structure must accompany autonomy |

### 4.2 The working rule

> High authority distance and low disagreement-directness do not mean empowerment is unwelcome. They mean it must be **granted rather than seized** — granted visibly, specifically, bounded, and by someone whose authority the team already accepts.

In such contexts an open invitation ("bring me your ideas") is not empowerment; it is a test most colleagues will decline to sit. The functioning equivalent is a named, bounded, publicly conferred mandate: *"Priya decides this class of exception up to this threshold. She does not need to ask me. If you disagree with her, take it to her."* Our practitioner judgement is that this single act moves more behaviour than a quarter of workshops — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§14), and testable inside the pilots via the decision-latency proxy.

### 4.3 Sponsorship: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** regional sponsors are selected on observed practice — leaders whose own teams already exhibit the four entitlements — rather than on rank.

We acknowledged in v1.0 that this backfires in several regions, then handed the choice back, which was no recommendation at all. The corrected position: the default stands, and a region wishing to depart from it does so through a **one-page note countersigned by the Regional MD and the programme director**, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner sponsor sits two or three levels below the Regional MD, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the senior figure as visible patron providing cover and air, the practitioner as the working engine. A junior sponsor without a senior patron will in several regions be read, reasonably, as the centre not taking the region seriously.

---

## 5. Using the regional cards well

### 5.1 What they are
Starting hypotheses about context, to be returned marked up within 45 days. They describe patterns we have observed in workplaces, not peoples.

### 5.2 What each card contains
Working hypothesis on the four axes · where the gap likely sits · behaviour to add · behaviour to drop · failure mode · **leading indicator observable by day 60** · legal or structural watch item.

### 5.3 The 60-day indicator, and why it is on every card
The failure modes that matter most — courteous non-adoption, affirmative response with no movement — are precisely the ones you cannot detect by asking. Each card therefore names an observable proxy visible within 60 days.

### 5.4 The supersession rule
**Where unit-level diagnostic data exists, it supersedes the card, and the card is retired for that unit.** Within-country variance in work values routinely exceeds between-country variance; function, site history and acquisition lineage frequently dominate nationality. This applies to every card, not only where we have noted it.

### 5.5 Scope note
Cards cover the fourteen clusters where we have wholly-owned or majority-controlled operations. Russia and Belarus are **out of scope** for this programme pending the Group's standing position on those entities; the programme director should not open a workstream there without a written instruction from the sponsor group.

---

## 6. Regional cards

### Card A — Anglosphere (US, Canada, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Low authority distance; direct disagreement acceptable; individual error attribution; moderate-to-high ambiguity tolerance |
| Likely gap | Not permission — **follow-through**. Voice is already loud; evidence that it changes anything is thin |
| Add | Visible closure loops: "here is what we did with what you told us, here is what we declined, and why" |
| Drop | Announcing empowerment. The region has heard it and discounts it |
| Failure mode | Ironic compliance; strong survey movement, unchanged decision latency |
| 60-day indicator | Ratio of raised items with a documented, dated response — target 80%+; skip-level uptake |
| Watch item | Strong individual error attribution and litigation exposure make Entitlement III hard: blame follows the name. US at-will/discipline documentation practice cuts against visible error absorption |
| Internal variance not to flatten | UK indirectness is closer to the Nordic-plus-hedging pattern than to US directness; Quebec sits closer to Card C than to the rest of Canada; the Australian register tolerates challenge to authority that would be career-limiting in the US |

### Card B — Germanic & Nordic (DE, AT, CH, NL, SE, DK, NO, FI)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Low-to-moderate authority distance, expertise-derived; very direct disagreement; system-oriented error attribution; **low ambiguity tolerance** |
| Likely gap | Vagueness. Autonomy without written scope reads as management failure, not freedom |
| Add | Precision — documented decision rights, thresholds, escalation triggers. More documentation produces more autonomy here, counter-intuitively |
| Drop | Motivational framing and aspirational language; actively corrosive of credibility |
| Failure mode | Formal structural objection: "not properly specified, and it touches co-determination" — and they will be right on both counts |
| 60-day indicator | Existence of a signed, unit-level decision-rights schedule; count of decisions taken against it |
| Watch item | **Works councils** — Betriebsrat, ondernemingsraad, Nordic union structures. Changes to appraisal criteria, working methods and monitoring are frequently co-determination matters. Engage as co-designers, not as clearance (§10.2) |
| Quiet opportunity | This cluster will build the best delegation architecture in the network. We would suggest letting it lead the design and having other regions borrow from it, rather than the reverse — a small reversal of the usual flow that would itself say something useful about the initiative |

### Card C — Latin Europe (FR, IT, ES, PT, GR)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Moderate-to-high authority distance; direct on substance, relationship-mediated in form; individual attribution with strong reputational weight; moderate ambiguity tolerance |
| Likely gap | Relational legitimacy. It must come from a leader people are personally loyal to, or it is noise from the centre |
| Add | Public named conferral (§4.

# Critic Review — *Global Supply Chain Resilience & Responsible Sourcing Programme, v1.0*

## Summary judgement

There is real quality here: the diagnosis table in §2.1, the live-switch test in §2.2(b), the self-audit of buyer conduct, and the disclosure amnesty are all better than what most procurement transformation papers contain. But the document cannot be sent to a steering group in this state. It stops mid-sentence in §3.5, roughly 60% of what it promises is missing, and one of its central design choices — a waiver route applied indiscriminately across all five floors — is legally unsound. Those two facts alone determine the assessment.

---

## Tier 1 — Blocking defects

**1. The paper is unfinished, and the missing parts are the ones that carry the decision.**
The text terminates at "triggers a time-bound rem". Absent are §§3.6–3.7 (alternative-form route), §4, §5, §6 (the cards), §7 (pilots), §8 (measurement, incentives, failure test detail), §9, §10, §11, §12, §13.1, §14. There are 38 forward references into sections that do not exist.

This is not a formatting problem. §2.3 states that the "uncomfortable question" of self-binding is "answered rather than deferred" and that the answer is §9. §9 is not there. The paper therefore makes precisely the move it criticises v1.0 of the empowerment paper for making. Similarly, the one-pager requests "three decisions — §12.5"; §12.5 does not exist, so the steering group is asked to approve $18.4M with no decision text, no assumptions, no gate structure and no critical-input list.

**2. The alternative-form waiver route is applied to a floor where no waiver can exist.**
Floor II (freely given labour, no worker-paid fees, no document retention, no wage withholding) is offered a "named-approver alternative-form route" on the same terms as traceability depth. That is a governance error with legal consequence. Forced-labour indicators are not a progressive standard: they sit under UFLPA rebuttable-presumption exposure, UK/Australian Modern Slavery reporting, the German LkSG, and the EU forced-labour regulation and CSDDD regime. An internally published register recording that the CPO approved a twelve-month departure from a forced-labour floor is a document that will be read aloud in a deposition, a customs detention proceeding, or an NGO report.

**Required fix:** split the floors into two classes.
- *Non-derogable* — Floor II core indicators, and the retaliation prohibition inside Floor III. No waiver, no register entry, only immediate escalation and remediation.
- *Progressive, with a dated closure plan rather than a waiver* — traceability depth (Tier 2 vs. smelter/farm level), grievance-channel maturity, alternate-capability qualification, exit sequencing.

The culture paper's "alternative form" construct was elegant *because* the underlying entitlements were behavioural. Transplanted onto legally-bounded human rights standards it becomes a liability-manufacturing device. This is the clearest evidence that the template was applied before the domain was fully thought through.

**3. The amnesty is a good idea presented in a form that cannot be adopted.**
"No scorecard penalty, no volume reduction, no cost recovery" for *any* self-disclosed labour finding, undeclared subcontractor, or **unapproved material substitution** is over-broad in three directions:

- *Legal carve-outs are missing.* Disclosures touching forced or child labour, sanctions/UFLPA-implicated inputs, bribery, or unlawful discharge can trigger mandatory reporting or criminal exposure. An amnesty cannot promise silence or inaction on these, and promising it destroys the amnesty's standing with regulators and customers.
- *Material substitution does not belong here.* Undeclared substitution is a product-safety, warranty, certification and recall issue. Bundling it with labour disclosure means the first serious substitution event collapses the whole scheme.
- *Moral hazard and privilege are unaddressed.* Nothing prevents a supplier banking a known problem and disclosing it on day 364. Nothing states where amnesty records sit, whether they attract legal privilege, who can access them, what customer flow-down notification obligations override the amnesty, or what happens at month 13 to problems disclosed but not yet remediated.

**Required fix:** amnesty covers commercial consequence only, never legal consequence; explicit scheduled exclusions; a "known-and-concealed-before-window" carve-out; a defined records architecture agreed with Legal and the external auditor before a single supplier hears the word.

---

## Tier 2 — Serious analytical gaps

**4. The failure test is constructed so that failure is almost impossible to declare.**
As written it requires the vanity metric to rise by ≥10 **and** (a) **and** (b) **and** (c). Any one condition failing to hold means no failure is declared. If the compliance index rises +9, nothing happens. If fee reimbursement reaches $260K while grievance closure and recovery time are both flat, nothing happens. Both cited disruptions came from below Tier 1, yet all five floors are drafted as if enforceable at "mapped sites" where the company has no contractual privity. The paper needs an explicit leverage taxonomy: directed buy / nomination, specification and approved-vendor control, joint purchasing with peers, co-investment, industry collective schemes, and — where none of these exist — honest acknowledgement that the floor is *observational* at that tier, not enforceable. **6. Resilience content is markedly thinner than ethics content.**
For a programme with "resilience" first in its title, the following are absent or reduced to a phrase:
- Criticality segmentation methodology (deferred to a §13.1 that doesn't exist) and time-to-survive / time-to-recover mapping.

- Supplier financial-distress monitoring — consistently a top-three disruption cause, entirely absent.
- Logistics, port, freight-lane and single-warehouse concentration.
- Natural-hazard and climate exposure of supplier sites; supplier cyber exposure.
- Tariff, sanctions and export-control scenario planning.
- The unresolved tension between resilience (more suppliers) and both cost and ethical oversight (fewer suppliers, deeper relationships). This trade-off is never named, let alone adjudicated.

**7. Cross-category supplier overlap is not addressed.** Devolving supplier choice, remediation sequencing, contract mechanics *and* the language used with suppliers to seven category leads and four plants guarantees that a supplier serving three categories receives three different standards, three audit visits, and three remediation demands — while the paper simultaneously commits to reporting "audit burden imposed" as a self-discipline metric. Define single-point supplier ownership and a mandatory-uniform contract layer before devolving the rest.

**8. The money is unanchored and the presentation is managed rather than analysed.**
No spend base, revenue, COGS, plant scale or category size is given, so $18.4M is uninterpretable — 0.1% of direct spend or 3%? The ~$46M working capital carries an unmentioned annual cost of roughly $3.7–4.6M plus obsolescence and scrap risk on qualification inventory. Asking the board *not* to add two numbers together reads as presentational management; the correct move is one total-cost-of-ownership view with funding routes and governance clearly distinguished on the same page.

**9. The decision architecture contradicts itself.** §2.2 says "no design freeze until it reports" (seven weeks), while the one-pager seeks $18.4M on 22 April. Resolve into an explicit stage gate: approve $640K diagnostic plus mobilisation and programme director recruitment on 22 April; full envelope, pilot scope and failure-test thresholds at a named gate after the diagnostic reports.

---

## Tier 3 — Weaknesses of construction and craft

**10. Governance is under-specified at three points.** "CPO sponsor, jointly accountable with COO" with no tiebreak invites stall on exactly the decisions that matter (spend more on qualification vs. hold cost-down). The programme director sits "in neither function" — so where, reporting to whom, with what budget authority? The CFO is absent despite $46M of working capital; the sustainability/reporting owner is absent despite CSRD and disclosure exposure that the paper itself flags as its top damage risk.

**11. Suppliers are absent from a programme about supplier partnership.** The paper extends the courtesy of pre-consultation to category leads and plant directors on precisely the reasoning that a programme arriving fully formed has already contradicted itself — then designs the entire supplier-facing architecture without a supplier advisory panel or any co-design step. Internally inconsistent.

**12. Worker-voice design gaps.** Who funds the channel (supplier funding exposes complainants), retaliation monitoring, remedy funding when the supplier cannot or will not pay, escalation where the site is Tier 2, and grievance-channel effectiveness criteria are all unaddressed. §10.6 is referenced for data protection but the operative risk — a complainant identified through case detail rather than name — needs design, not a cross-reference.

**13. "Audit-score inflation correction" is asserted with no method.** As with the parent paper's "acquiescence correction", stating a correction without stating its basis is decoration. Give at least the approach (e.g., unannounced-audit delta, worker-voice divergence coefficient, auditor-firm fixed effects).

**14. The evidence key is used inconsistently and its legend is missing.** [O], [E] and [J] appear four or five times; the great majority of contestable assertions — the 70/30 weighting, the 12-month amnesty duration, the 65%/35% offset schedule, the 180-day traceability refresh — carry no marker. Mark them or drop the device.

**15. An actionable finding is stated and then walked past.** "1,780 of 1,834 Tier-1 suppliers" signed the code. That means 54 suppliers did not sign and apparently continued to supply. That is an immediate, cheap, checkable action item and it is used only as rhetorical furniture.

**16. Register and tone.** The house style is effective in places but tips into mannerism, and several phrases are lifted verbatim from the empowerment paper — "the line most often omitted and most often fatal", "Demonstrated, never announced", "unchanged Tuesday morning". A steering group whose members read both papers will notice, and will discount the analysis accordingly. The opening comparison to the culture programme is of no operational use to this audience; make it a footnote or cut it. "We would gently ask" appears twice in two pages; once is a courtesy, twice is a tic.

---

## The six changes I would make first

1. **Finish the paper**, or re-issue it honestly as a partial draft with the missing sections listed and dated. §9 in particular must exist before this circulates, because the paper's credibility claim rests on it.
2. **Split the floors** into non-derogable and progressive; remove Floor II from any waiver route.
3. **Re-engineer the amnesty**: commercial consequence only, scheduled legal carve-outs, substitution removed, records and privilege architecture agreed with Legal and the external auditor first.
4. **Rebuild the failure test** on OR-logic, with thresholds set as post-diagnostic parameters and coverage-based rather than absolute-dollar metrics.
5. **Add the missing resilience half**

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** our whistleblowing channel, and not a legal reporting route. The two are separately named, separately routed, separately governed. Conflating them creates legal exposure on one side and chills genuine reporting on the other (§10.4). Data from worker channels is held so that it cannot be used to identify a complainant to their employer (§10.6).

### 3.4 Floor IV — good-faith disclosure is absorbed, not punished
**Floor:** during the 12-month amnesty window, a supplier that discloses an undeclared subcontractor, a labour finding, a fee-charging recruiter, or an unapproved material substitution receives a remediation plan and **no scorecard penalty, no volume reduction, no cost recovery**. What we find ourselves carries consequence. What they bring us does not.

Each category should be able to name, per quarter, at least one specific disclosure it absorbed, and the category team should be able to describe it. Demonstrated, never announced.

*This is the floor that will attract the most internal objection and it is the one we would defend hardest.* The alternative is what we have now: a network with a strong incentive to keep problems on the far side of the questionnaire **[J]**.

### 3.5 Floor V — remediate before exit; exit responsibly
**Floor:** discovery of a labour or environmental finding triggers a time-bound rem

# Critic Review — *Global Supply Chain Resilience & Responsible Sourcing Programme, v1.0*

## Summary judgement

There is real quality here: the diagnosis table in §2.1, the live-switch test in §2.2(b), the self-audit of buyer conduct, and the disclosure amnesty are all better than what most procurement transformation papers contain. But the document cannot be sent to a steering group in this state. It stops mid-sentence in §3.5, roughly 60% of what it promises is missing, and one of its central design choices — a waiver route applied indiscriminately across all five floors — is legally unsound. Those two facts alone determine the assessment.

---

## Tier 1 — Blocking defects

**1. The paper is unfinished, and the missing parts are the ones that carry the decision.**
The text terminates at "triggers a time-bound rem". Absent are §§3.6–3.7 (alternative-form route), §4, §5, §6 (the cards), §7 (pilots), §8 (measurement, incentives, failure test detail), §9, §10, §11, §12, §13.1, §14. There are 38 forward references into sections that do not exist.

This is not a formatting problem. §2.3 states that the "uncomfortable question" of self-binding is "answered rather than deferred" and that the answer is §9. §9 is not there. The paper therefore makes precisely the move it criticises v1.0 of the empowerment paper for making. Similarly, the one-pager requests "three decisions — §12.5"; §12.5 does not exist, so the steering group is asked to approve $18.4M with no decision text, no assumptions, no gate structure and no critical-input list.

**2. The alternative-form waiver route is applied to a floor where no waiver can exist.**
Floor II (freely given labour, no worker-paid fees, no document retention, no wage withholding) is offered a "named-approver alternative-form route" on the same terms as traceability depth. That is a governance error with legal consequence. Forced-labour indicators are not a progressive standard: they sit under UFLPA rebuttable-presumption exposure, UK/Australian Modern Slavery reporting, the German LkSG, and the EU forced-labour regulation and CSDDD regime. An internally published register recording that the CPO approved a twelve-month departure from a forced-labour floor is a document that will be read aloud in a deposition, a customs detention proceeding, or an NGO report.

**Required fix:** split the floors into two classes.
- *Non-derogable* — Floor II core indicators, and the retaliation prohibition inside Floor III. No waiver, no register entry, only immediate escalation and remediation.
- *Progressive, with a dated closure plan rather than a waiver* — traceability depth (Tier 2 vs. smelter/farm level), grievance-channel maturity, alternate-capability qualification, exit sequencing.

The culture paper's "alternative form" construct was elegant *because* the underlying entitlements were behavioural. Transplanted onto legally-bounded human rights standards it becomes a liability-manufacturing device. This is the clearest evidence that the template was applied before the domain was fully thought through.

**3. The amnesty is a good idea presented in a form that cannot be adopted.**
"No scorecard penalty, no volume reduction, no cost recovery" for *any* self-disclosed labour finding, undeclared subcontractor, or **unapproved material substitution** is over-broad in three directions:

- *Legal carve-outs are missing.* Disclosures touching forced or child labour, sanctions/UFLPA-implicated inputs, bribery, or unlawful discharge can trigger mandatory reporting or criminal exposure. An amnesty cannot promise silence or inaction on these, and promising it destroys the amnesty's standing with regulators and customers.
- *Material substitution does not belong here.* Undeclared substitution is a product-safety, warranty, certification and recall issue. Bundling it with labour disclosure means the first serious substitution event collapses the whole scheme.
- *Moral hazard and privilege are unaddressed.* Nothing prevents a supplier banking a known problem and disclosing it on day 364. Nothing states where amnesty records sit, whether they attract legal privilege, who can access them, what customer flow-down notification obligations override the amnesty, or what happens at month 13 to problems disclosed but not yet remediated.

**Required fix:** amnesty covers commercial consequence only, never legal consequence; explicit scheduled exclusions; a "known-and-concealed-before-window" carve-out; a defined records architecture agreed with Legal and the external auditor before a single supplier hears the word.

---

## Tier 2 — Serious analytical gaps

**4. The failure test is constructed so that failure is almost impossible to declare.**
As written it requires the vanity metric to rise by ≥10 **and** (a) **and** (b) **and** (c). Any one condition failing to hold means no failure is declared. If the compliance index rises +9, nothing happens. If fee reimbursement reaches $260K while grievance closure and recovery time are both flat, nothing happens. Convert to OR-logic across the substantive proxies, and treat the compliance-index rise as an *aggravating* condition rather than a gate.

Separately, the metrics themselves are weak:
- *"$250K reimbursement network-wide"* is an absolute currency figure with no denominator. It rewards finding a few large cases and is silent on coverage. Replace with: % of high-risk mapped sites where a fee assessment was completed, and % of identified fee-payers reimbursed in full within 90 days, worker-confirmed.
- *"Time-to-recover improves <25%"* is set against a baseline that does not exist yet — §2.2(b), the live-switch test, is what will produce it. You cannot set the threshold before the diagnostic runs. State it as a post-diagnostic gate parameter.
- *"Worker-confirmed grievance closure"* uses confirmation of *receipt* as the proxy for closure. Receipt is not remedy. Use the UNGP Principle 31 effectiveness criteria and measure outcome satisfaction and non-retaliation at 90 days.

**5. No leverage model below Tier 1 — which is where the paper says the failures originated.**
Both cited disruptions came from below Tier 1, yet all five floors are drafted as if enforceable at "mapped sites" where the company has no contractual privity. The paper needs an explicit leverage taxonomy: directed buy / nomination, specification and approved-vendor control, joint purchasing with peers, co-investment, industry collective schemes, and — where none of these exist — honest acknowledgement that the floor is *observational* at that tier, not enforceable. Without this, Floors I–III are aspirational precisely where they matter.

**6. Resilience content is markedly thinner than ethics content.**
For a programme with "resilience" first in its title, the following are absent or reduced to a phrase:
- Criticality segmentation methodology (deferred to a §13.1 that doesn't exist) and time-to-survive / time-to-recover mapping.
- **Design-for-resilience.** Single-sourcing is created in engineering, at specification and part-approval, not in procurement. There is no engineering workstream, no part-standardisation or second-source-ready spec requirement, no PPAP/qualification-cycle compression work. This is the largest structural omission.
- Supplier financial-distress monitoring — consistently a top-three disruption cause, entirely absent.
- Logistics, port, freight-lane and single-warehouse concentration.
- Natural-hazard and climate exposure of supplier sites; supplier cyber exposure.
- Tariff, sanctions and export-control scenario planning.
- The unresolved tension between resilience (more suppliers) and both cost and ethical oversight (fewer suppliers, deeper relationships). This trade-off is never named, let alone adjudicated.

**7. Cross-category supplier overlap is not addressed.** Devolving supplier choice, remediation sequencing, contract mechanics *and* the language used with suppliers to seven category leads and four plants guarantees that a supplier serving three categories receives three different standards, three audit visits, and three remediation demands — while the paper simultaneously commits to reporting "audit burden imposed" as a self-discipline metric. Define single-point supplier ownership and a mandatory-uniform contract layer before devolving the rest.

**8. The money is unanchored and the presentation is managed rather than analysed.**
No spend base, revenue, COGS, plant scale or category size is given, so $18.4M is uninterpretable — 0.1% of direct spend or 3%? The ~$46M working capital carries an unmentioned annual cost of roughly $3.7–4.6M plus obsolescence and scrap risk on qualification inventory. Asking the board *not* to add two numbers together reads as presentational management; the correct move is one total-cost-of-ownership view with funding routes and governance clearly distinguished on the same page.

**9. The decision architecture contradicts itself.** §2.2 says "no design freeze until it reports" (seven weeks), while the one-pager seeks $18.4M on 22 April. Resolve into an explicit stage gate: approve $640K diagnostic plus mobilisation and programme director recruitment on 22 April; full envelope, pilot scope and failure-test thresholds at a named gate after the diagnostic reports.

---

## Tier 3 — Weaknesses of construction and craft

**10. Governance is under-specified at three points.** "CPO sponsor, jointly accountable with COO" with no tiebreak invites stall on exactly the decisions that matter (spend more on qualification vs. hold cost-down). The programme director sits "in neither function" — so where, reporting to whom, with what budget authority? The CFO is absent despite $46M of working capital; the sustainability/reporting owner is absent despite CSRD and disclosure exposure that the paper itself flags as its top damage risk.

**11. Suppliers are absent from a programme about supplier partnership.** The paper extends the courtesy of pre-consultation to category leads and plant directors on precisely the reasoning that a programme arriving fully formed has already contradicted itself — then designs the entire supplier-facing architecture without a supplier advisory panel or any co-design step. Internally inconsistent.

**12. Worker-voice design gaps.** Who funds the channel (supplier funding exposes complainants), retaliation monitoring, remedy funding when the supplier cannot or will not pay, escalation where the site is Tier 2, and grievance-channel effectiveness criteria are all unaddressed. §10.6 is referenced for data protection but the operative risk — a complainant identified through case detail rather than name — needs design, not a cross-reference.

**13. "Audit-score inflation correction" is asserted with no method.** As with the parent paper's "acquiescence correction", stating a correction without stating its basis is decoration. Give at least the approach (e.g., unannounced-audit delta, worker-voice divergence coefficient, auditor-firm fixed effects).

**14. The evidence key is used inconsistently and its legend is missing.** [O], [E] and [J] appear four or five times; the great majority of contestable assertions — the 70/30 weighting, the 12-month amnesty duration, the 65%/35% offset schedule, the 180-day traceability refresh — carry no marker. Mark them or drop the device.

**15. An actionable finding is stated and then walked past.** "1,780 of 1,834 Tier-1 suppliers" signed the code. That means 54 suppliers did not sign and apparently continued to supply. That is an immediate, cheap, checkable action item and it is used only as rhetorical furniture.

**16. Register and tone.** The house style is effective in places but tips into mannerism, and several phrases are lifted verbatim from the empowerment paper — "the line most often omitted and most often fatal", "Demonstrated, never announced", "unchanged Tuesday morning". A steering group whose members read both papers will notice, and will discount the analysis accordingly. The opening comparison to the culture programme is of no operational use to this audience; make it a footnote or cut it. "We would gently ask" appears twice in two pages; once is a courtesy, twice is a tic.

---

## The six changes I would make first

1. **Finish the paper**, or re-issue it honestly as a partial draft with the missing sections listed and dated. §9 in particular must exist before this circulates, because the paper's credibility claim rests on it.
2. **Split the floors** into non-derogable and progressive; remove Floor II from any waiver route.
3. **Re-engineer the amnesty**: commercial consequence only, scheduled legal carve-outs, substitution removed, records and privilege architecture agreed with Legal and the external auditor first.
4. **Rebuild the failure test** on OR-logic, with thresholds set as post-diagnostic parameters and coverage-based rather than absolute-dollar metrics.
5. **Add the missing resilience half**

### How we would ask you to use this

Three notes, then the substance.

**First, what changed from v1.0 and why.** The reviewers were right on three points that went to the design rather than to the drafting, and we would rather record that plainly than absorb it quietly.

1. v1.0 offered a single waiver route across all five floors. That was wrong. A standard concerning forced labour cannot carry a waiver, and an internal register recording that an officer of this company approved a twelve-month departure from one would be a document read back to us in a customs proceeding or an NGO report. 2. The disclosure amnesty in v1.0 promised more than we are lawfully able to promise. **Second, the cards.** The cluster cards in §6 are **working hypotheses about supply structures and site conditions, offered so that they can be corrected**. They describe patterns we have observed in supply flows, not countries and not the people who live in them. Where a category lead or plant holds real diagnostic data — an unannounced assessment, a worker-voice sample, a qualification study — that data supersedes the card and the card is retired for that flow (§5.4). A card returned unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet taken place, and we would come back for it.

**Third, two courtesies we would ask the steering group to extend before this travels further.**

- That the seven category leads, the four plant directors and the two engineering chiefs see §§3, 4, 9 and 13 and have time to respond in their own way, through their own line, before the board pack is assembled. A programme that devolves sourcing judgement and then arrives in a category fully formed has already contradicted itself, and colleagues will notice that before they notice anything else.

The single likeliest cause of avoidable damage here is not a supply failure. It is a well-meant public commitment that becomes a disclosure liability, or a supplier questionnaire that creates a written record we cannot later stand behind.

*A note on suppliers themselves: v1.0 designed a supplier-facing architecture without consulting a supplier, while arguing that programmes arriving fully formed contradict themselves. That inconsistency is corrected in §11.5 — a supplier advisory panel of nine, convened before Gate 2, with two seats reserved for Tier-2 firms.*

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Resilience is a purchased option rather than an attitude; and responsible sourcing is an information problem before it is a compliance problem. **[J]** — considered practitioner assertion, not a finding. The steering group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement; the key is at §14 and is now applied throughout rather than decoratively.

The failure we are trying to avoid is documented in our own last three years: a supplier code signed by 1,780 of 1,834 Tier-1 suppliers **[O]**; an audit pass rate above 90% **[O]**; and two disruptions in eighteen months that neither the code nor the audits anticipated, both originating below Tier 1 **[O]**, with combined recovery cost of $23.6M and 41 days of line stoppage across two plants **[O]**. That combination is not a coverage gap. It is evidence that we have measured the wrong things accurately.

### 1.2 What we are not claiming

We are not claiming that this programme prevents disruption. It shortens recovery and reduces the number of surprises **[J]**. We are not claiming it makes the supply base ethical; it makes conditions in it visible and gives us a route to act, which is a smaller and more honest claim **[J]**. And we are not claiming the floors are enforceable at every tier — §4.2 sets out, tier by tier, where we hold leverage and where a floor is honestly **observational** rather than enforceable. v1.0 blurred that line, and blurring it would have embarrassed us in front of the very colleagues we need.
